lessons: Hook lines that directly state a relatable bodily reaction or surprising natural phenomenon (such as 'Fresh pineapple is literally eating you back') achieve strong start retention above 1.0.
Generic introductory filler phrases like 'They are not just there to look cool' or 'They look like similar fruits' trigger immediate drop-offs, often losing over 30% of viewers.
Pause prompts and explicit countdowns ('three, two, one') do not inherently retain viewers better; videos relying on them still experience steep early losses unless the premise is deeply engaging.

Complex historical or metabolic explanations introduced mid-video (e.g., Greenland shark metabolism or deep cellular structures) successfully hold late-stage audiences when the initial hook is exceptionally strong.
Repetitive phrasing or stating the exact same mechanism twice in succession (seen in the guardrail video) results in heavy viewer abandonment at the drop points.
worst_moment_types: Vague descriptive statements or filler sentences that fail to advance the core explanation
Redundant restatements of a mechanism already explained in the hook
Abrupt transitions into dense technical or biological details without a clear bridge
best_hook_types: Direct, high-stakes declarations that challenge common assumptions (e.g., animal or bodily defenses targeting the human body)
Immediate framing of a counter-intuitive physical anomaly (such as extreme longevity or temperature resistance)
